paper_title: Self-WSP: Can Language Models Improve Themselves Through Weight-Space Programming?

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Frontier language models can now read and edit the weights of a neural network much like code and thereby improve a small model, an approach known as Weight-Space Programming (WSP). We further explore applying WSP to a language model itself, which we call Self-WSP. Specifically, Qwen3.5-0.8B reads its own weights, proposes an edit, and then continues with the edited weights as both problem solver and editor. We find many cases of genuine self-improvement. Self-edits can raise GSM8K accuracy from 11.8% to 62.2% and MATH500 accuracy from 7.0% to 32.2%, sometimes by changing only 16 parameters, and in some cases repeated self-editing keeps improving the model. A closer look, however, reveals that these gains lack interpretability. The model shows little understanding of the edits it makes, and WSP driven by random search sometimes performs comparably. Self-WSP thus holds promise as a path toward recursive self-improvement (RSI), but realizing this promise requires further exploration.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content: A system that improves its own intelligence, and with it its ability to improve itself further, is longstanding idea known as recursive self-improvement (RSI) (Good, 1966; Schmidhuber, 2007). Language models already improve themselves in several ways. They train on rationales, data or rewards they generate themselves (Zelikman et al., 2022; Huang et al., 2023; Yuan et al., 2024), rewrite the code that calls them (Zelikman et al., 2024; Zhang et al., 2026), or learn to write their own finetuning data (Zweiger et al., 2025). In each case, however, the model changes its weights only indirectly, through data, code or training. Weight-Space Programming (WSP) offers more direct route. Takehi et al. (2026) show that GPT-6 Astra, hereafter GPT-6, can read the weights of neural network and edit them much like code. 1 Figure 1: The Self-WSP loop. One model plays two roles. As the editor, it reads its own current weights and proposes an edit. As the solver, it answers practice questions using copy of the weights with the edit applied. The outer loop checks whether more answers are correct, and if so the copy replaces the current weights, so that the next proposal comes from the edited model. Asked to make Qwen3.5-0.8B better at math without gradients, it traced the small models failures to single direction in two MLP layers, removed that direction from 0.016% of the weights, and raised MATH500 accuracy from 7.9% to 48.1%. Their experiments leave open whether model can improve its performance by editing its own weights. We study this possibility directly. In Self-WSP, Qwen3.5-0.8B edits itself. As Figure 1 shows, the model reads its own weights, proposes an edit, and continues with the edited weights, both as the solver that answers questions and as the editor that proposes the next edit. fixed outer loop decides which edits to keep, and for this purpose we divide questions into three kinds. Practice questions come from the training split with reference answers, and are used to test whether an edit helps. Validation questions also come from the training split but are never shown to the editor, and serve only to select models after the search. The test sets are the standard GSM8K and MATH500 test questions, used only for the final evaluation. With this setup we ask four questions, and Figure 2 summarizes the test accuracy of the best model of each method. Figure 2: Test accuracy of the best model of each method. Each method contributes its Top-1 model, the one with the largest gain on validation questions. In the Self-WSP experiments of Section 2, the shuffled interface lists the tensor catalog in random order and the ordered interface lists it by layer. Continued runs let the best shuffled models keep editing themselves under the ordered interface. Bold values mark the highest Self-WSP score shown for each dataset. Random search replaces the editor with random sampler under the same budget as the shuffled interface. The single random edit is the best of the edits tested individually on the original model, as described in Section 5. GPT-6s two edits come from Takehi et al. (2026) and are re-evaluated in our pipeline. Can model improve itself through its weights? Yes. Self-edits raise GSM8K accuracy about fivefold and MATH500 accuracy more than threefold, sometimes by changing handful of numbers. Does the model know what it is doing? Hardly. It edits whichever tensors are listed first, reuses numbers it has just read, and often gives hallucinated explanations. Many of the edits it keeps make the model worse. Can random edits do the same? To some extent. Random search matches self-editing on GSM8K but falls short on MATH500, and the best single random edit is as good as the simpler of GPT-6s two published edits. Can Self-WSP keep improving the model? In lucky cases. Continued self-editing lifts the best models further, to more than four times the original MATH500 accuracy, while typical runs make little further progress. Self-improvement through the weights is therefore within reach of even 0.8B model. Its current successes, however, come mostly from search and selection rather than from understanding, and closing this gap is the main challenge ahead.

sections.title: 2 Self-Weight-Space Programming
sections.content: Self-WSP is loop in which single model alternates between editing its weights and using them. standard attention. linear-attention layer stores what it has read in fixed-size state and forgets old information at rate set by its weights. As the editor, the model proposes edits with thinking turned off. As the solver, it answers math questions with thinking turned on, using the sampling settings of Takehi et al. (2026). Both roles always use the current weights, so every kept edit changes both how the model solves problems and how it then proposes the next edit. Reading its own weights. The editor sees catalog of the 318 tensors it may edit, which covers all 24 layers and gives the name and shape of each tensor. After it picks one or two tensors, it receives their shape, statistics such as the mean and standard deviation, up to 64 of their values with positions, and the norms of their rows and columns. It also sees how the current model does on batch of practice questions, including the reference answers and the end of the models responses for few examples. This matches the setting of Takehi et al. (2026), where GPT-6 also reads the actual weight values, can check its edits only on practice questions from the training split, and never sees the test sets. The difference is that GPT-6 could analyze the weights freely in Python environment, whereas our editor sees only the information above, precomputed by the system. Appendix describes the full interface. One model, two roles. Both roles are played by Qwen3.5-0.8B (Qwen Team, 2026), 24-layer model in which three of every four layers use linear attention (Yang et al., 2025b) and the fourth uses Writing its own weights. model this small does not reliably follow output formats, so the editor writes its edits as JSON under grammar built from the tensor shapes (Willard and Louf, 2023; Geng et al., 2023). Each proposal contains one or two edits. An edit selects block of consecutive entries, rows or columns in tensor and applies one of seven operations to it. It can set the block to zero, multiply it by number, add number, fill it with number, redraw it at random from the tensors mean and standard deviation, remove direction, or apply short NumPy expression. Removing direction applies only to matrices. The editor names one column of the matrix as the direction, and every selected column subtracts its component along that direction, scaled by coefficient. coefficient of 1 removes this component entirely. GPT-6s most effective edit also removes direction, but computes it from the models activations. The grammar guarantees the format but not the content, and edits that repeat an earlier one, rescale whole tensor uniformly or change no value are discarded at once. We call the remaining edits valid edits. Keeping edits. Each run proceeds in rounds from starting model. Every round has fixed budget, the largest number of valid edits it may try, and the editor proposes edits until the budget is spent. round also ends early after 24 proposals or after several valid edits in row are rejected. Each valid edit is first applied to copy of the weights and then checked on two disjoint practice batches. It is kept only if the edited model solves enough additional questions on the two batches combined without doing worse on either, in which case the copy becomes the new current weights. The budget, the batch size and the required gain depend on the interface, which we describe next. Two interfaces. We run the loop with two interfaces, which differ mainly in how the tensor catalog is ordered. The shuffled interface lists all tensors in random order, and the editor picks tensors directly. It uses 32 practice questions per batch, keeps any edit that gains single answer in total, and runs three rounds with budgets of 4, 6 and 12 valid edits. The ordered interface lists the tensors in layer order, and the editor first picks layer and then tensors within it. It uses 128 questions per batch, requires total gain of at least three answers, and spends budget of 8 valid edits per round. Appendix gives the full settings. sections.title: 5 Can Random Edits Do the Same?
sections.content: If lucky proposals drive the gains, random edits might do as well. We test this by replacing the editor with random sampler that calls no model. Random search. For each proposal, the sampler draws one tensor uniformly from the catalog, or two with probability one fifth. It then picks random layout, start and count, and random operation with its value, choosing among setting to zero, scaling, adding or filling small number, redrawing and removing direction. Appendix gives the exact distributions. The sampler runs through the same loop with the same selection rules as the original model answers with some randomness, and merely answering again with another random seed moves its score on these 128 questions by few points. We call this movement sampling noise and take its 5th to 95th percentile as the noise range, shown as the grey band in Figure 7. An edit inside the band cannot be told apart from doing nothing. As Figure 7 shows, most random edits fall inside the grey band or below it. On GSM8K, 78 edits fall below the band and only 24 rise above it. Large edits that touch tens of thousands to millions of weights do the most damage, and almost every kind of operation hurts on average. few random edits nevertheless help. We rescore the best eight per dataset on 512 further questions from the practice pool and test the winner. It reaches 22.3% on GSM8K by scaling 4,096 weights of convolution by 2, and 14.0% on MATH500 by scaling 64 rows of query projection by 2. Appendix gives the sampling details. GPT-6s simpler edit is random edit. One of GPT-6s two published edits sets 256 columns of the attention output matrix of layer 15 to zero. Such an edit lies within the range of the single random edits, although the sampler would draw it only about once in 130 million tries. In our evaluation it scores 22.0% on GSM8K and 13.8% on MATH500, as good as the best single random edits, and in the screening it merely ranks among the better random edits. GPT-6s stronger edit removes direction computed from the models activations, which lies outside what the sampler can produce. Where self-editing beats chance. Self-editing does beat chance in places. In the same screening, the best self-edited model of the shuffled interface gains more than all 352 random edits on both datasets. On MATH500, the selected continued +4 models gain up to 17.2 points in the screening, more than twice the best random edit, and selfediting also beats random search with the same budget. Its proposals are thus better than random draws, though only modestly, and not because the model knows why they work.

sections.title: 7 Discussion
sections.content: The outer loop does much of the work. The model proposes every edit and is changed by every kept one, but the outer loop does the rest. Using practice questions with reference answers, it decides which edits to keep, when to stop and which run to test. Self-WSP is therefore best seen as search in which the model supplies the proposals, and these proposals beat random ones on MATH500 but merely match them on GSM8K. Why small edits go long way. As its model card warns, Qwen3.5-0.8B often gets stuck repeating itself while thinking, and the original model fails to finish within its 32k-token budget on about 90% of questions. Almost every answer that an edit makes correct is one the original model never finished, and across all evaluated models accuracy falls almost linearly with the share of unfinished answers. Any edit that breaks the repetition can therefore raise accuracy sharply. This fits reports that few parameters can have outsized effects (Yu et al., 2024), that correcting small fraction of thinking tokens during reasoning clearly raises accuracy (Ling et al., 2026b), and that Qwen models improve at math even when trained with spurious rewards (Shao et al., 2026). It may also explain why GPT-6 could not improve Gemma 3 270M, model that rarely repeats itself (Takehi et al., 2026). Toward genuine self-improvement. model that improves itself because it understands its weights must act on what it reads. Natural next steps include tools for analyzing weights, which GPT-6 had and our editor lacked, training model to propose edits (Zweiger et al., 2025), and solvers whose failures run deeper than repetition. Progress along this path is best measured against random search with the same interface and budget, and reported together with spot-check runs. Figure 8: Continued self-editing. sections.title: 8 Related Work
sections.content: Large language models. Scaling models and data has given language models broad abilities (Kaplan et al., 2020; Brown et al., 2020; Touvron et al., 2023; OpenAI, 2023; Yang et al., 2025a). Chain-ofthought prompting elicits intermediate reasoning steps (Wei et al., 2022). Reinforcement learning trains models to reason at length (Guo et al., 2025), and test-time scaling trades more inference compute for higher accuracy (Snell et al., 2025; Wan et al., 2026), for example by searching for better reasoning paths (Ling et al., 2026b). Mathematical reasoning is common testbed for testing and improving these abilities (Cobbe et al., 2021; Hendrycks et al., 2021; Qin et al., 2024). These advances rely on training, prompting or extra inference compute, whereas Self-WSP lets model directly rewrite its own weights without gradients. Self-improvement. Models can refine their outputs with their own feedback (Madaan et al., 2023) or generate more creative data and train on the best of it (Zhong et al., 2024), although they often fail to correct their own reasoning (Huang et al., 2024). Other work lets model rewrite its own prompts, agent designs or running logic and keeps the better versions (Fernando et al., 2024; Hu et al., 2025; Yin et al., 2025). All of these methods act on data, prompts or code, whereas Self-WSP acts on the weights themselves. The idea of neural network that modifies its own weights is old (Schmidhuber, 1993), and modern self-referential weight matrices can rewrite themselves at run time (Irie et al., 2022). These networks, however, are trained for this purpose, while Self-WSP lets general-purpose language model read and write its own weights from instructions in natural language. Editing and writing weights. Model editing changes facts or behaviors through targeted weight updates (Meng et al., 2022, 2023), trained editor networks (Mitchell et al., 2022), arithmetic on weight differences (Ilharco et al., 2023) or the removal of single directions (Arditi et al., 2024), usually guided by interpretability (Elhage et al., 2021). Pruning research uses weight statistics such as norms to judge which parameters can be removed, finds that these statistics often fail to tell parameters apart (Huang et al., 2021), and turns to search to blend several criteria (He et al., 2021). Hypernetworks use one network to generate the weights of another (Ha et al., 2017), and language models have been used to explain the neurons of other models (Bills et al., 2023). WSP instead asks generalpurpose language model to read and write weights toward goal stated in natural language (Takehi et al., 2026). Fan et al. (2026) improved Qwen3.527Bs math accuracy using frozen copy as editor. Other WSP studies include Kundu (2026); Hu et al. (2026); Fischetti (2026); Salloum and Ali (2026). Propose and select. Our loop resembles methods in which language model proposes candidates and an evaluator keeps the best. Such methods have been applied to prompts, pipelines, programs and algorithms (Yang et al., 2024; Khattab et al., 2024; Romera-Paredes et al., 2024; Novikov et al., 2025), and language model can even act directly as an evolution strategy over numerical parameters (Lange et al., 2024). Evolutionary search has also been used to find ways of merging the weights of several models (Akiba et al., 2025). In Self-WSP, the language model that proposes the candidates is itself the object being optimized. Gradient-free and random baselines. Evolution strategies and zeroth-order methods optimize networks with forward passes alone (Salimans et al., 2017; Malladi et al., 2023), now even for language models with billions of parameters (Qiu et al., 2026). Random search is strong baseline in hyperparameter optimization and reinforcement learning (Bergstra and Bengio, 2012; Mania et al., 2018), and in benchmark compression randomly drawn subset of questions often comes close to the full benchmark (Ling et al., 2026a). Repetition and overthinking are known failures of text generation and reasoning models (Holtzman et al., 2020; Xu et al., 2022; Chen et al., 2025). Our results connect these threads. When models fail mainly through repetition, random perturbations can also be useful.

sections.title: 9 Conclusion
sections.content: We asked whether language model can improve itself by editing its own weights. Our results show that 0.8B model can. Its own edits raise GSM8K accuracy fivefold and MATH500 accuracy more than fourfold, sometimes by changing handful of numbers, and in lucky runs continued self-editing keeps paying off. Despite the improvements, the model shows little understanding of its edits, and random edits sometimes achieve comparable gains. Self-WSP is promising path toward RSI, and turning it into reliable ability is the work ahead.

sections.title: Limitations
sections.content: We study single small model on two math benchmarks, and its main weakness, repetitive thinking, is unusually easy to repair. The outer loop uses the reference answers of practice questions to decide which edits to keep, so the improvement is supervised. The ordered interface was designed after we had seen the results of the shuffled one. We have not yet run random search under it, nor tested the source of the layer-0 preference directly by reversing the catalog. Finally, the comparison with GPT-6 is only indicative, since GPT-6 used different tools, feedback and budgets.

sections.title: Ethics Statement
sections.content: Self-editing of weights may introduce behaviors that math benchmark does not measure. All edits in this study are logged and reproducible and concern 0.8B model evaluated on public benchmarks. We use Qwen3.5-0.8B under the Apache-2.0 license, GSM8K and MATH under the MIT license, and the GPT-6 edits under CC BY 4.0.

sections.content: You are Qwen3.5-0.8B. Improve your own numerical weights for mathematics, without gradients or training. The target always solves questions with thinking enabled. Practice feedback is optimization data; tests are hidden. First choose one decoder layer, then one or two tensors of that layer to read. You will receive statistics, sampled real values and row/column norms of the current weights. Then propose an explicit edit. The host stops at the fixed proposal budget or patience limit; do not stop yourself. Positions and values must be your own decisions; no successful repair is provided. Repairing an internal failure is allowed; do not make the target skip thinking or close it immediately regardless of the question. Allowed layouts: flat entries, whole rows, or whole columns. start/count select consecutive indices with circular wrap. Operations: zero; scale by value; add value; fill with value; normal replacement with this tensor mean and abs(value) times its standard deviation; project subtracts value times the component along normalized column direction you choose; expression computes the replacement with bounded NumPy. Supported expressions include array slicing, + - * / @, np.mean/std/sum/outer/dot/array/reshape and np.linalg.norm. The expression must return scalar or the same shape as S.
